turns.t: Hello, doctor. It's my eyes, the contact lenses, they've gone uncomfortable. I forgot to say on the phone, I wear them every day.
What does uncomfortable mean?
Dry, and sort of scratchy by the afternoon. I have to take them out by about four, and my eyes feel tired.
How long have you worn contact lenses? ~
Eight years, but it's only got bad recently. I'm forgetting how long. Since March, I think? Or April. ~
That's fine. What are you putting in your eyes?
Lubricating drops, four times a day. Hypromellose, I think the packet says. Does that sound right?
That's right. And the other tablets you mentioned on the form?
Cetirizine, 10 mg once a day, for my hay fever.
Good. How many hours a day are you in lenses, and where, a screen, air conditioning? ~
Ten, eleven hours. I'm at a computer all day, in an air-conditioned office. ~
That's the classic recipe for dry eyes. How do you clean and store the lenses? ~
I use the solution, and I change the case every month. Or every two months. Sometimes three. ~
That's a little long, the case should be changed monthly. And do you ever sleep in them? ~
Once or twice, if I'm tired. ~
Please try not to, that raises the risk of infection. ~
I'll try. ~
Let me have a look at your eyes. Chin on the rest. ~
Right.
Fine. There's no infection and nothing is scratched. Your eyes are a little dry on the surface. ~
So it's not serious? ~
Not serious. I'd say it's dry eye related to your lens wear, made worse by the screen and the air conditioning.
What do I do? ~
Wear glasses on some days to give your eyes a rest, take the lenses out by the time you get home, and use preservative-free drops.
The drops I've got, are they preservative-free? ~
Not the ones you've got, ask the pharmacist for single-use vials, and keep using them. ~
Right, that's useful. ~
Blink fully when you're at the screen, and look away every twenty minutes, twenty seconds.
I will, I'll set an alarm. ~
I'd like to see you again in six weeks, to see if the lenses are more comfortable.
Six weeks. Thank you. ~
